{{Short description|Fewest dependent columns in a matrix}}
In [[mathematics]], more specifically in [[linear algebra]], the '''spark''' of a <math>m \times n</math> [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] <math>A</math> is the smallest integer <math>k</math> such that there exists a set of <math>k</math> columns in <math>A</math> which are [[Linear independence|linearly dependent]]. If all the columns are linearly independent, <math>\mathrm{spark}(A)</math> is usually defined to be 1 more than the number of rows. The concept of matrix spark finds applications in [[Error correction code|error-correction codes]], [[compressive sensing]], and [[matroid theory]], and provides a simple criterion for maximal sparsity of solutions to a [[system of linear equations]].

The spark of a matrix is [[NP-hard]] to compute.<!-- Sourced in body. ~Duckmather -->

==Definition==
Formally, the spark of a matrix <math>A</math> is defined as follows:
{{Equation box 1
|indent =
|title=
|equation = {{NumBlk|:|<math>\mathrm{spark}(A) = \min_{d \ne 0} \|d\|_0  \text{  s.t.  }  A d = 0 </math>|{{EquationRef|Eq.1}}}}
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
where <math>d</math> is a nonzero vector and <math>\|d\|_0</math> denotes its number of nonzero coefficients<ref name="TP14" /> (<math>\|d\|_0</math> is also referred to as the size of the support of a vector). Equivalently, the spark of a matrix <math>A</math> is the size of its smallest ''circuit'' <math>C</math> (a subset of column indices such that <math>A_C x = 0</math> has a nonzero solution, but every subset of it does not<ref name="TP14" />).

If all the columns are linearly independent, <math>\mathrm{spark}(A)</math> is usually defined to be <math>m+1</math> (if <math>A</math> has ''m'' rows).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Higham|first1=Nicholas J.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MvI8CgAAQBAJ&dq=%22spark%22+%22mathematics%22+%22matrix%22&pg=PA824|title=The Princeton Companion to Applied Mathematics|last2=Dennis|first2=Mark R.|last3=Glendinning|first3=Paul|last4=Martin|first4=Paul A.|last5=Santosa|first5=Fadil|last6=Tanner|first6=Jared|date=2015-09-15|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-1-4008-7447-7|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Manchanda|first1=Pammy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Cr06DwAAQBAJ&dq=%22spark%22+%22mathematics%22+%22matrix%22&pg=PA35|title=Industrial Mathematics and Complex Systems: Emerging Mathematical Models, Methods and Algorithms|last2=Lozi|first2=René|last3=Siddiqi|first3=Abul Hasan|date=2017-10-18|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-981-10-3758-0|language=en}}</ref>{{Dubious|date=May 2024|Definition in case of full column rank}}

By contrast, the [[rank (linear algebra)|rank]] of a matrix is the largest number <math>k</math> such that some set of <math>k</math> columns of <math>A</math> is linearly independent.<ref name=pnas/>

==Example==
Consider the following matrix <math>A</math>.

<math>
A=
\begin{bmatrix}
 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\
 1 & 2 & 0 & 2 \\
 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\
 1 & 0 & -3 & 4
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

The spark of this matrix equals 3 because:
* There is no set of 1 column of <math>A</math> which are linearly dependent.
* There is no set of 2 columns of <math>A</math> which are linearly dependent.
* But there is a set of 3 columns of <math>A</math> which are linearly dependent. The first three columns are linearly dependent because <math>\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\2\\0\end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}</math>.
==Properties==
If <math>n\geq m </math>, the following simple properties hold for the spark of a <math>m \times n</math> matrix <math>A</math>:

*<math>\mathrm{spark}(A) = m+1 \Rightarrow \mathrm{rank}(A) = m</math> (If the spark equals <math>m+1</math>, then the matrix has full rank.)
*<math>\mathrm{spark}(A) = 1 </math> if and only if the matrix has a zero column.
*<math>\mathrm{spark}(A) \le \mathrm{rank}(A) + 1 </math>.<ref name=pnas/>

==Criterion for uniqueness of sparse solutions==
The spark yields a simple criterion for uniqueness of sparse solutions of [[System of linear equations|linear equation systems]].<ref>{{cite book
  | last = Elad
  | first = Michael
  | title = Sparse and Redundant Representations From Theory to Applications in Signal and Image Processing
  | url = https://archive.org/details/sparseredundantr00elad_246
  | url-access = limited
  | pages = [https://archive.org/details/sparseredundantr00elad_246/page/n44 24]
  | year = 2010}}</ref>
Given a linear equation system <math>A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}</math>. If this system has a solution <math>\mathbf{x}</math> that satisfies <math>\|\mathbf{x}\|_{0} < \frac{\mathrm{spark}(A)}{2}</math>, then this solution is the [[Sparse matrix|sparsest]] possible solution. Here <math>\|\mathbf{x}\|_{0}</math> denotes the number of nonzero entries of the vector <math>\mathbf{x}</math>.

==Lower bound in terms of dictionary coherence==
If the columns of the matrix <math>A</math> are normalized to unit [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]], we can lower bound its spark in terms of its dictionary coherence:<ref>{{cite book
  | last = Elad
  | first = Michael
  | title = Sparse and Redundant Representations From Theory to Applications in Signal and Image Processing
  | url = https://archive.org/details/sparseredundantr00elad_246
  | url-access = limited
  | pages = [https://archive.org/details/sparseredundantr00elad_246/page/n46 26]
  | year = 2010}}</ref><ref name=":0" />
:<math>\mathrm{spark}(A) \ge 1+\frac{1}{\mu(A)} </math>.

Here, the dictionary coherence <math>\mu(A)</math> is defined as the maximum correlation between any two columns:
:<math>\mu(A)=\max_{m \neq n} |\langle a_m,a_n \rangle| = \max_{m\neq n}\frac{|a_m^{\intercal} a_n|}{||a_m||_2||a_n||_2} </math>.

==Applications==
The minimum distance of a [[linear code]] equals the spark of its [[parity-check matrix]].

The concept of the spark is also of use in the theory of [[compressive sensing]], where requirements on the spark of the measurement matrix are used to ensure stability and consistency of various estimation techniques.<ref name=pnas>{{Citation
  | last1 = Donoho
  | first1 = David L.
  | author-link = David Donoho
  | last2 = Elad
  | first2 = Michael
  | author2-link = 
  | title = Optimally sparse representation in general (nonorthogonal) dictionaries via ℓ<sup>1</sup> minimization
  | journal = Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.
  | volume = 100
  | issue = 5
  | pages = 2197–2202
  | date = March 4, 2003
  | doi = 10.1073/pnas.0437847100
  | id =
  | pmid = 16576749
  | pmc = 153464 | bibcode = 2003PNAS..100.2197D
  | doi-access = free
 }}</ref> It is also known in [[matroid theory]] as the [[matroid girth|girth]] of the vector matroid associated with the columns of the matrix. The spark of a matrix is [[NP-hard]] to compute.<ref name=TP14>{{cite journal|last=Tillmann|first=Andreas M.|author2=Pfetsch, Marc E. |title=The Computational Complexity of the Restricted Isometry Property, the Nullspace Property, and Related Concepts in Compressed Sensing|journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory|date=November 8, 2013|volume=60|issue=2|page=1248&ndash;1259|doi=10.1109/TIT.2013.2290112|arxiv=1205.2081|s2cid=2788088}}</ref>
